# Can referee "105" see any part of player "85"?

## Short answer

**No — almost certainly not.** Player 85 is squarely inside the field of view that
referee 105 is facing, but he is eclipsed by the head of the man in the black
jacket (the coach/official) who is standing right in front of the referee. From
105's own eye position, 85 sits almost exactly behind that man's head, so no part
of 85 — head, torso, legs or the helmet he is holding up — reaches 105's eyes.

## What is in the picture

* The referee with **105** on his back is in the right foreground, photographed
  from behind. He is therefore facing *away* from the camera, into the scene, and
  his head is turned very slightly to **his left** (both ears are visible around
  the cap's centre seam, but the seam sits closer to his right ear, implying a
  turn of roughly 10° to his left).
* Directly in front of him, about 1.2–1.8 m away and slightly to **his left**,
  stands the man in the black jacket, facing him and gesturing with his right
  hand. The referee's body occludes that man's left shoulder, confirming the
  referee is the nearer of the two.
* Player **85** (white jersey, black pants, holding his helmet up in both hands)
  is far away in the background at the left of the frame, standing on the field
  just inside the boundary wall, next to teammate 74.

## Why 85 is not visible to 105

**1. Direction is not the problem — 85 is in front of him.** Reconstructing the
scene from the image (using head widths for depth, the feet/horizon for the
background distances, and a camera focal length that the result turns out not to
depend on), player 85 lies about **12° to the referee's left** of straight ahead.
That is well inside his central vision, and it is roughly the direction his head
is already turned. So this is not a "he's facing the wrong way" case.

**2. The coach's head is at that exact same bearing.** From the referee's eye
position, the black-jacketed man's head also lies about **12° to his left** —
the same direction as 85, within a fraction of a degree. The coach's head is only
~1.2–1.8 m away, so it subtends roughly ±3.5° of the referee's view, while 85,
about 15 m further off, subtends only about ±0.8°. The big near object completely
swallows the small far one.

**3. This is a parallax effect the photo hides.** In the photograph the two look
well separated (the coach's face is ~210 pixels to the right of 85), but the
camera is roughly 2 m *behind* the referee's head and about 0.1–0.3 m to his left.
Shifting the viewpoint forward to the referee's eyes swings the near head about
10° further left, while the distant player shifts only ~2°. That closes the gap
entirely. A useful way to state it: the coach's head casts a "blind spot" cone
that is roughly **2 m wide by the time it reaches 85's distance**, and 85 —
about 0.45 m wide including his raised arms and helmet — sits within ~0.1 m of
the centre of that cone, with roughly 0.7 m of clearance on either side.

**4. Nothing peeks over the top or under the bottom either.** Every sightline
from 105's eyes to any part of 85 — from the top of the helmet he is holding up
down to his shoes — crosses the coach's plane at a height of roughly 1.56–1.72 m,
which is exactly the band occupied by the coach's forehead, face and neck (his
head top is ~1.78 m, his chin ~1.61 m, his shoulders ~1.54 m). No ray to 85
passes above the coach's head or below his shoulder line, and the rays aimed at
85's feet pass through the coach's neck/collar rather than beside it.

**5. Nothing else is in the way, and nothing else needs to be.** The coach's
outstretched right hand is about 30 cm too low and well to the left of the
sightline; the space between the coach and 85 is empty green field; the crowd and
the advertising boards are all *behind* 85 (he stands in front of the wall, his
legs overlapping the "SPORTSRADIO 1250" board). The coach's head alone does the
blocking.

## Confidence and the one caveat

The conclusion is a geometric reconstruction from a single photo, so I tested it
against measurement error. Randomising every input over generous ranges (head
sizes 15–17.5 cm, ±2–3 px on every pixel measurement, focal length 1100–2400 px,
camera height 1.45–1.90 m, horizon row 206–246, referee head turn 0–18°) gives:

* **~70% of reconstructions: 85 is completely hidden.**
* **~95%: less than 10% of 85's width would be visible** (a sliver at one edge).
* Only ~2% put more than half of him in view.

So the answer is "no" with good confidence, and in the small minority of cases
where something is visible it would be no more than a thin edge of his shoulder
or arm, not a recognisable portion of the man.

The honest caveat is that the blocker is a head, not a wall: the eclipse is only
a few centimetres wide at the coach's face. If the referee leaned or stepped just
~6 cm sideways, or if either man shifted slightly, player 85 would come straight
back into view. At the instant this frame was taken, though, the coach's head is
directly on the line between referee 105's eyes and player 85, and 105 cannot see
any portion of him.
